title: 58th sitting of the 20th Majlis
summary: The 58th sitting of the 20th Majlis opened on 9 December 2024 at 09:02. After routine items, the Speaker referred the President's list of nominees for the Maldives Inland Revenue Authority board to the Economic Committee, and a government bill on foreign currency was read for the first time. Most of the part was the debate on the government's bill to amend the Drugs Act (Act 17/2011), where members backed the bill, argued about enforcement, border checks, courts and prevention, and the sponsor closed the debate, with the vote left for the day's voting time. After a recess (10:30 to 11:01), the Judiciary Committee presented reports on bills amending the Penal Code and the Criminal Procedure Act, and the report on a third bill was just starting when this part ends. The text has dropped marks and jumbled digits, so the attendance figures are read as printed. This part covers the end of the morning session and the afternoon voting. Members debated two committee reports: one on appointing Fuad Thowfeek as Maldives ambassador to the Kingdom of Thailand, and one on appointing Maryam Insha Faisal to the National Integrity Commission. Both were backed by the speakers, and after a short procedural exchange about attendance the chair broke for lunch. After the break six votes were held: a drugs law amendment bill was accepted for study, three bills passed, and both appointments were approved with no votes against.

items.title: Votes on items debated so far
items.outcome: drugs bill accepted 57-0 and sent to Judiciary Committee; Penal Code, Criminal Procedure and Legal Assistance bills passed 58-0; both appointments approved 58-0

speakers.name: Ibrahim Shujau
positions: Backed the bill, criticised past governments for not installing airport and port scanners, and welcomed plans to scan all containers at the port.
Asked that seized drugs be destroyed publicly and that new drug types be written into the law during committee stage.
On item 9.2, backed the report and said police powers must not be used for political ends.
Fully backed the Thailand ambassador nominee as well qualified and respected.

speakers.name: Husnee Mubarik
positions: In the debate, backed the bill but questioned whether remand centres and 24-hour rules for control-delivery operations can work in practice.
Supported letting new drug types be added to the schedule by presidential decree on the National Drug Council's advice, and holding drug-cafe owners liable.
As Judiciary Committee rapporteur, presented the committee reports on items 9.1, 9.2 and the start of 9.3.

speakers.name: Abdul Rahman
positions: Backed the aim but said enforcement agencies lack the capacity and integrity to be given wide powers, and that drug trade and corruption are linked.
Objected to amendments that let the state take property before guilt is proven, and said they may conflict with the Constitution.
Called for the toughest penalties on those who use children in the drug trade.

speakers.name: Hussain Shareef
positions: Said drug use among young people keeps rising and that the first step is raising children with firm Islamic belief.
Argued that school-age religious upbringing, not new laws alone, is the base of any lasting fix.

speakers.name: Hassan Mufeed Abdul Gadir
positions: Backed the bill and said the law needs to be tougher and workable, with stronger treatment and drug-court processes.
Rejected claims that earlier governments did nothing on the problem and urged cooperation across parties.

speakers.name: Mohamed Abbas
positions: Backed the bill but said weak enforcement, not a lack of laws, is the main reason the trade continues, and alleged links between some police and traffickers.
Criticised the courts for delays and called for stronger checks on bulk goods arriving by boat.
Asked the government to provide shelter for people sleeping rough in Malé.

speakers.name: Hussain Ziyad
positions: Backed the amendments but said the real gaps are enforcement, prevention and living conditions.
Questioned treating users inside overcrowded prisons instead of remand centres and said high quantity thresholds let big dealers escape.

speakers.name: Ahmed Nazim
positions: Recalled the 2011 law and its drug-court model and said the problem is still unsolved after thirteen years.
Gave border examples (a boat with its tracker switched off, parcels, airport baggage) and asked for stronger police and customs capacity.

speakers.name: Ahmed Xamyr
positions: Backed the bill, citing UN and WHO survey figures on drug use among working-age men.
Called for a multi-sector approach covering border control, prevention, treatment and sharing data between agencies.

speakers.name: Saudulla Hilmy
positions: Called drugs the biggest social problem and said families raised it at every door during the election campaign.
Said laws only help if enforced and that all institutions and the Majlis should work with the government.

speakers.name: Abdul Gafoor Moosa
positions: Said the amendments are good but filing them is not action and that no government has yet solved the problem.
Raised the MMPRC case and said the law must apply equally to everyone, criticising investigators and courts for letting suspects go.

speakers.name: Abdul Latheef Mohamed
positions: Fully backed the bill and said past governments' efforts produced no results.
Said easy profit keeps the trade going and asked courts and investigators to deliver cases much faster.

speakers.name: Yoosuf Nasheed
positions: As sponsor, thanked the President and said the UNODC cooperation was not used between 2018 and 2023.
Explained the added definitions, the change to rehabilitation orders, proceeds-of-crime provisions and border-smuggling rules, and asked the committee to weigh Customs and Police comments.

speakers.name: Mohamed Dawoodh
positions: Presented the Foreign Relations Committee report on the Thailand ambassador nominee, listing the institutions consulted and the committee's unanimous recommendation.

speakers.name: Hussain Riza Adam
positions: Presented the Independent Institutions Committee report on the National Integrity Commission nominee, covering the checks, interview and scoring process.

speakers.name: Hussain Sameer
positions: Raised a point of order on the party make-up of members present in the chamber.

decisions: Minutes of sittings 51/2024 to 55/2024 were declared accepted with no amendments.
The President's nominees for the Maldives Inland Revenue Authority board were referred to the Economic Committee.
A government bill on foreign currency was read for the first time.
Debate on the bill amending the Drugs Act (Act 17/2011) was closed; the vote was left for the day's voting time.
Judiciary Committee reports on the Penal Code and Criminal Procedure Act amendment bills were presented and the bills read a third time.
Drugs Act (17/2011) amendment bill accepted for consideration, 57 yes, and sent to the Judiciary Committee
Penal Code (9/2014) amendment bill passed, 58 yes, 0 no
Criminal Procedure Act (12/2016) amendment bills passed together, 58 yes, 0 no
Mutual Legal Assistance in Criminal Matters Act (2/2015) amendment bill passed, 58 yes, 0 no
Fuad Thowfeek approved as ambassador to the Kingdom of Thailand, 58 yes, 0 no
Maryam Insha Faisal approved as National Integrity Commission member, 58 yes, 0 no
Next sitting set for 10 December 2024 at 9:00

votes.what: Accept for consideration the bill to amend the Drugs Act (17/2011)
Pass the bill to amend the Penal Code (9/2014)
Pass the two bills to amend the Criminal Procedure Act (12/2016)
Pass the bill to amend the Mutual Legal Assistance in Criminal Matters Act (2/2015)
Appoint Fuad Thowfeek as ambassador to the Kingdom of Thailand
Appoint Maryam Insha Faisal to the National Integrity Commission
